newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: Israel complying with U.N. torture probe - source.
newsitem.headline: Israel complying with U.N. torture probe - source.

text.p: Israel has begun to collaborate with the U.N. Committee against Torture, which is concerned about a recent Israeli High Court ruling that appeared to sanction police brutality there, U.N. sources said on Thursday.
The chairman of the committee, Alexis Dipanda Mouelle, wrote to the Israeli government last month and the U.N. sources said he had received a letter from Israel's ambassador in Geneva.
"There has been a reply indicating a willingness to collaborate," a U.N. source told Reuters. "It is a first step."
Treatment of detainees in Israel has become a big issue after footage of police abusing six Palestinians shown on Israeli television last month prompted the suspenion of two paramilitary policemen.
"The (Israeli) authorities are following the question. Our letter has not been ignored. But we don't know at this stage whether it will be complete cooperation," the source added.

Israel's High Court overturned an interim court order on November 14, which had forbidden Israel's Shin Bet secret police to use "physical force" against two Palestinian detainees while interrogating them.
Both were suspected of belonging to radical Islamist groups Jihad and Hamas believed to responsible for deadly bomb attacks.

The committee, which oversees compliance with the Convention against Torture, told Israeli officials in the letter that the ruling seemed to be "incompatible" with the 1972 pact -- a major rights instrument.
It reminded the Jewish state, which signed the treaty in 1991, that "no exceptional circumstances whatsoever" -- neither war nor internal political instability -- justified torture.
Israel's diplomatic mission to the United Nations in Geneva started to comply by making texts and information provided by its Ministry of Justice available, U.N. sources said.

The committee had asked Israel to provide a special report by January 31 as a matter of urgency, so that its experts could consider the matter at their next semi-annual session starting on April 28. It hoped Israeli officials would take part.
"It will be important to see whether more information follows and whether Israel will send a delegation to the next session to have a true debate on the issue," the source said.

Israel had been due to submit a routine report to the committee on its compliance with the Convention by November 1. No report has been handed in so far. The report would normally be discussed at the next Geneva session from April 28-May 11.
